functions: Distance–time graph: an upward straight line; its gradient is speed
Speed–time graph: an upward straight line; its gradient is acceleration
figure.description: Draw two separate graphs. In the first, put distance on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. In the second, put speed on the vertical axis and time on the horizontal axis. Show an increasing straight line on each.
figure.title: Gradients of distance–time and speed–time graphs

steps: Draw distance–time axes with distance vertically and time horizontally. The gradient of the line is change in distance divided by change in time, so it represents speed.
Draw speed–time axes with speed vertically and time horizontally. The gradient of the line is change in speed divided by change in time, so it represents acceleration.
A steeper line on a distance–time graph means greater speed; a steeper line on a speed–time graph means greater acceleration.
items.finalAnswer: The gradient of a distance–time graph represents speed. The gradient of a speed–time graph represents acceleration; the diagrams show these gradients as the slopes of their respective lines.

figure.description: Draw the representative line 4 cm long, at 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹. Add an arrowhead and label it 400 m s⁻¹.
figure.title: Velocity vector

steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 60° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 4 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 400 m s⁻¹.
items.finalAnswer: The representative line is 4 cm long at 60° to the positive x-axis, labelled 400 m s⁻¹, using the scale 1 cm = 100 m s⁻¹.

figure.description: Draw the representative line 5 cm long, at 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis. Scale: 1 cm = 10 N. Add an arrowhead and label it 50 N.
figure.title: Force vector

steps: Choose the scale 1 cm = 10 N.
Draw the positive x-axis as the reference direction.
From the origin, measure 120° anticlockwise from the positive x-axis and draw a 5 cm line in that direction.
Put an arrowhead at the end and label the line 50 N.
items.finalAnswer: The representative line is 5 cm long at 120° to the positive x-axis, labelled 50 N, using the scale 1 cm = 10 N.

functions: Two equal, opposite, parallel forces act along different lines of action
figure.description: Show a rigid bar with the equal forces applied at separated points: the upper arrow points right and the lower arrow points left. Their lines of action are parallel and separated by distance d. The forces form a couple.
figure.title: A couple: zero resultant force, non-zero resultant torque

steps: Draw a rigid bar and show two equal forces F acting parallel to one another at different points.
Draw one force to the right and the other to the left.
The resultant force is F − F = 0.
Because their lines of action are separated by distance d, their torques act in the same rotational direction. The resultant torque (couple) has magnitude Fd + Fd = 2Fd, which is not zero.
items.finalAnswer: The two equal and opposite forces have zero resultant force, but because they act along different lines of action they produce a non-zero resultant torque.

steps: Given: m_A = 30 kg, d_A = 2 m; m_B = 40 kg, d_B = 1.5 m; take g = 10 N kg⁻¹.
Weight of A: W_A = m_Ag = 30 × 10 = 300 N.
Moment due to A = W_A d_A = 300 × 2 = 600 N m (anticlockwise).
Weight of B: W_B = m_Bg = 40 × 10 = 400 N.
Moment due to B = W_B d_B = 400 × 1.5 = 600 N m (clockwise).
The moments are equal and opposite, so the net moment is 600 − 600 = 0 N m.
items.finalAnswer: Each side produces a moment of 600 N m (equivalently 60 kgf m using kgf). The moments are equal and opposite, so the see-saw is in rotational equilibrium. The printed 60 corresponds to the kgf m convention.

functions: At the first hilltop: gravitational potential energy high, kinetic energy low
Downhill: potential energy changes into kinetic energy
At the bottom: kinetic energy high, potential energy low
Uphill: kinetic energy changes into potential energy
figure.description: Draw a cyclist at the top of one hill, descending to a valley and climbing the next hill. Label the first top 'high potential energy, low kinetic energy', the downhill 'potential energy → kinetic energy', the valley 'kinetic energy maximum', and the climb 'kinetic energy → potential energy'.
figure.title: Energy changes as a cyclist travels over two hills

steps: At the top of the first hill, the cyclist has high gravitational potential energy and relatively low kinetic energy.
As the cyclist moves downhill without pedalling, gravitational potential energy decreases and is converted into kinetic energy; the cyclist speeds up.
At the bottom of the valley, kinetic energy is greatest and potential energy is least.
As the cyclist climbs the next hill, kinetic energy is converted back into gravitational potential energy and the cyclist slows down.
If energy losses are neglected, the cyclist can reach the same height on the next hill.
items.finalAnswer: The cyclist’s potential energy changes into kinetic energy while going downhill. While climbing the next hill, kinetic energy changes back into potential energy.

functions: F(x) = F for 0 ≤ x/L ≤ 1
F(x) = 2F for 1 ≤ x/L ≤ 3
figure.description: Use displacement on the horizontal axis and force on the vertical axis. The graph is horizontal at F from displacement 0 to L, then horizontal at 2F from L to 3L. Label the axes x and force, and mark L and 3L on the x-axis.
figure.title: Force–displacement graph

steps: Work done equals the area under a force–displacement graph.
For the first distance L, the force is F: W₁ = F × L = FL.
For the further distance 2L, the force is 2F: W₂ = 2F × 2L = 4FL.
Total work done = W₁ + W₂ = FL + 4FL = 5FL.
items.finalAnswer: The force–displacement graph has a level F section from 0 to L and a level 2F section from L to 3L. The total work done, equal to the area under the graph, is 5FL.

steps: Pascal’s Law states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of its container.
A hydraulic press applies this law: pressure applied to a small piston is transmitted through the fluid to a larger piston, producing a greater output force.
A hydraulic lift uses the pressure transmitted through oil to raise a heavy vehicle.
In hydraulic brakes, pressure applied at the brake pedal is transmitted by brake fluid to the wheel brakes.
items.finalAnswer: Pascal’s Law: pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished throughout the fluid and to the container walls. Its applications include hydraulic presses, hydraulic lifts and hydraulic brakes.

functions: End A: north pole; viewed from A, conventional current around the solenoid is anticlockwise
End B: south pole; viewed from B, conventional current around the solenoid is clockwise
figure.description: Draw a cell, switch and solenoid in series. Show the steel bar inside the coil, with A at the left end and B at the right. Connect the cell polarity so the conventional current appears anticlockwise when viewed from end A. Label A as N and B as S.
figure.title: Magnetising a steel bar in a solenoid

steps: Place the steel bar AB inside a solenoid and connect the solenoid, a cell and a switch in series.
Choose the current direction so that, when viewed from end A, the current around the solenoid is anticlockwise.
By the end rule for a solenoid, an anticlockwise current at an end makes that end a north pole.
Therefore A becomes N and the opposite end B becomes S.
items.finalAnswer: The diagram shows a steel bar AB inside a solenoid connected in series with a cell and switch. Conventional current is anticlockwise when viewed from A, making A the north pole and B the south pole.

functions: Left magnet: S–N; right magnet: N–S, so like poles face across the gap
Field in the gap from each facing N pole is equal and opposite at the midpoint
outside: Show field lines leaving each facing N pole and curving outward toward the magnets' outer S poles
figure.description: Draw two similar bar magnets end-to-end with N poles facing across the gap: left magnet S–N and right magnet N–S. Place a compass at the midpoint. Sketch the magnetic field lines bowing outward between the like poles; the fields from the two magnets cancel at the midpoint, where the compass aligns with Earth's north–south field.
figure.title: Like poles facing across a gap

steps: Label the poles so that the same poles face one another across the gap; for example, use N–N facing, with the outer ends both S.
Draw magnetic field lines emerging from each N pole and curving around towards the S poles.
At the midpoint, the fields due to the two similar magnets are equal and opposite, so their resultant is zero.
With the magnets’ fields cancelling there, the compass needle aligns with Earth’s magnetic field in the north–south direction.
items.finalAnswer: The magnets have like poles facing across the gap (for example, N–N). Their magnetic fields cancel at the midpoint, so the compass aligns north–south under the influence of Earth’s magnetic field.

functions: At each solenoid, the end facing O is N and the outer end is S
Viewed from O, current around each solenoid is anticlockwise
Field at O due to each solenoid points radially inward; if one is switched off, the resultant points outward toward that solenoid
figure.description: Place four identical solenoids north, east, south and west of O, all at equal distance. Mark the end of each solenoid facing O as N and its outer end as S. Draw the conventional current anticlockwise when each coil is viewed from O. Show equal field arrows at O pointing inward from all four solenoids.
figure.title: Four solenoids arranged around O

steps: Place the four similar solenoids at equal distances north, east, south and west of O, with equal currents.
Make the end of every solenoid facing O a north pole. By the end rule, the conventional current is anticlockwise when each coil is viewed from O.
The four equal magnetic fields at O point towards O from their respective solenoids. Their vector sum is zero when all four are on.

If one solenoid is switched off, the fields of the other three have a resultant opposite to the field that the removed solenoid produced. This resultant points from O towards the switched-off solenoid.
items.finalAnswer: Make all four ends facing O north poles, with current anticlockwise when viewed from O. When any one solenoid is switched off, the resultant field at O points towards that solenoid.

functions: Strong field: magnetic field lines close together
Weak field: magnetic field lines far apart
Uniform field: straight, parallel, equally spaced magnetic field lines
outside: Magnetic field lines form closed curves and never intersect
figure.description: Draw three examples: several closely spaced parallel field lines for a strong field; widely spaced lines for a weak field; and equally spaced, straight parallel lines for a uniform field. Add arrows to show the direction of the field.
figure.title: Magnetic field strength and field-line spacing

steps: The strength of a magnetic field is indicated by the density of its magnetic lines of force.
Where field lines are close together, the magnetic field is strong; near the poles of a magnet the lines are crowded.
Where field lines are far apart, the magnetic field is weak.
In a uniform magnetic field, the lines are straight, parallel and equally spaced.
Magnetic field lines form closed curves and never intersect.
items.finalAnswer: Magnetic field strength is shown by the closeness of the magnetic lines of force: close lines indicate a strong field, widely spaced lines indicate a weak field, and equally spaced parallel lines represent a uniform field.

functions: The breaker switch is in series with the supply and load
Excess current energises the electromagnet and opens the contacts
figure.description: Draw a supply, breaker contacts and load in series. Show the breaker contacts mechanically linked to an electromagnet coil, so that excessive current pulls the contacts apart and opens the circuit. Label the switch 'circuit breaker'.
figure.title: Circuit breaker

steps: A circuit breaker is an automatic safety switch that breaks a circuit when the current becomes excessive.
It is connected in series with the circuit it protects.
During an overload or short circuit, the large current produces a strong magnetic effect in the breaker’s electromagnet.
The electromagnet attracts an armature, separating the contacts and opening the circuit.
After the fault is removed, the breaker can be reset.
items.finalAnswer: A circuit breaker is an automatic switch that protects a circuit from excessive current. Excess current strengthens its electromagnet, which opens the contacts and breaks the circuit.
